content.text: Nuclear fusion is the process that powers the Sun and all stars. Small nuclei combine to form larger ones, releasing enormous energy. While fusion has been achieved in hydrogen bombs and experimental reactors, creating controlled fusion for power generation remains one of the greatest technological challenges—and promises—of our time.

Nuclear fusion requires extremely high temperatures (millions of degrees) to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei. At these temperatures, matter exists as plasma. Containing this plasma is the main challenge for fusion power on Earth.

Do not confuse fission and fusion. Fission = splitting (think 'fission = fissure = crack/split'). Fusion = joining (think 'fuse together'). Both release energy, but from opposite processes and with very different fuels and conditions.
— They're opposite processes. Fission splits large nuclei; fusion joins small ones.
— The reaction requires precise conditions. Any disruption stops the reaction immediately.
"We just need to make the Sun's conditions"
— Actually, we need HOTTER than the Sun because we can't match its density and time.
— The reaction produces neutrons, and reactor materials can become radioactive, but waste is much less problematic than fission.
— Even if successful, it will take decades to deploy widely and won't replace all other energy sources.

Fusion produces far less radioactive waste than fission and uses abundant hydrogen as fuel. However, the extreme temperatures required (over 100 million degrees Celsius) make it enormously difficult to achieve on Earth. The Sun can sustain fusion because of its immense gravitational pressure.
Fusion: combining light nuclei to form heavier ones + energy
Requires extreme temperature (~100 million °C) to overcome electrostatic repulsion
Energy from mass defect: E = Δmc²
Advantages: abundant fuel, no CO₂, less waste, inherently safe
Challenges: achieving and maintaining conditions, net energy gain
ITER project working towards demonstrating feasibility
Commercial fusion power possibly 2050s or later
Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a single heavier nucleus, with the release of energy due to a mass defect (the products have less mass than the reactants).
— definition must include joining, light nuclei, and energy release (definition)
— balance A and Z on both sides (calculation)

Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other due to electrostatic (Coulomb) force. At low temperatures, nuclei lack sufficient kinetic energy to overcome this repulsion. At millions of degrees, the kinetic energy is high enough for nuclei to approach close enough that the strong nuclear force (which only acts at very short range) can bind them together.

Fission can be triggered by slow neutrons at room temperature; it only requires a critical mass of fissile material. Fusion requires temperatures above 100 million degrees C to overcome electrostatic repulsion between nuclei. Maintaining these extreme conditions and confining the plasma (which would vaporise any container) is an enormous engineering challenge with no equivalent in fission.

Magnetic confinement (tokamak): strong magnetic fields hold the hot plasma in a doughnut-shaped chamber, preventing it from touching the walls. Inertial confinement: powerful lasers compress a small fuel pellet from all sides, briefly achieving the temperature and density needed for fusion.
— two distinct approaches to plasma containment (description)

The D-T reaction has the lowest ignition temperature of any fusion reaction (~100 million degrees C), making it the most achievable. It also releases the most energy per reaction (17.6 MeV). Deuterium is abundant in seawater, and tritium can be bred from lithium in the reactor.
— lowest threshold + highest energy yield + fuel availability (reasoning)

Fusion advantages over fission: fuel (deuterium from seawater) is virtually limitless; the main product is helium, which is non-radioactive, so there is far less long-lived waste; a fusion reactor cannot melt down because any loss of conditions instantly stops the reaction; no chain reaction risk; no CO2 emissions.
— waste, safety, fuel supply all favour fusion (comparison)
